extracted.intended_audience: young British gentlemen / people learning to argue politely in company
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on how to conduct oneself when disputing in social/company settings: when to avoid argument, how to present reasons, how to keep temper, when to retreat, and how to act as an impartial moderator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disputes as much as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid Disputes as much as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To appear easy and well-bred in Conversation, it requires more wit and more good humour to improve than to contradict the notions of another. The author frames avoidance as the preferred default in company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give reasons with coolness and modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: When obliged to enter an Argument, give your Reasons with the utmost Coolness and Modesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coolness and modesty scarce ever fail of making an impression on the hearers. Being neither dogmatical nor showing by actions or words that you are full of yourself will increase acceptance of your view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be dogmatical or show arrogance
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid being dogmatical or showing by words/actions that you are full of yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humility makes others more heartily rejoice at your victory; arrogance alienates. If you are neither dogmatical nor vain, your success is more welcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retreat gracefully when pinched
rubrics_metrics.description: If pressed in argument, make your retreat with good grace by admitting you were never positive and are glad to be better informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tactic (recommended as Socratical) prevents being caught in absurdity and preserves reputation: you seem only to desire information while possibly attempting to persuade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Socratic way of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a questioning/Socratic approach: scarce affirm anything and appear to desire information rather than force assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By scarcely affirming, you are hard to catch in absurdity; you may be endeavouring to bring over another to your opinion, yet seem only to seek information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep your temper; avoid passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is more unjust or ridiculous than to be angry with another because he is not of your opinion; avoid falling into passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider differing interests, education, and means that shape opinions; ask what your opinion might have been under your adversary's biases. Passion is an 'infallible maxim' to avoid — it gives advantage to antagonists and makes you forget good reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for information/truth rather than mere victory
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose to yourself the true end of Argument, which is Information; search purely after Truth rather than the honour of Victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the goal is truth, it becomes almost indifferent where you find it. Contending for victory alone leads to passion and poor conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity those who cannot apprehend your reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: If an adversary cannot comprehend your reasons, regard him with pity rather than anger; thank nature for your clearer understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguing for reputation makes victory easier, but you should neither be angry nor scornful when others give weak reasons—compassion is more appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anger is wasted among equals; it harms its possessor
rubrics_metrics.description: Among your equals no one values your Anger, which only preys upon its Master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anger gains nothing in company and is inconsistent with prudence and ease; do not punish yourself emotionally when you meet a fool or knave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act as an impartial moderator when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing the part of Moderator (impartial) procures esteem and less envy from the company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being impartial gives opportunity to sift things to the bottom, display judgment, and make handsome compliments to each contending party—this role increases esteem and avoids taking sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: When victorious, do not press the advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have gained a Victory, do not push it too far; let people see it's in your power but that you are too generous to use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's sufficient to show your power; excessive triumphing harms reputation and the company. Modesty after victory preserves social harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat and violence cause one to forget good reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: After an Argument is over, many weighty Reasons are recollected which heat and violence made one utterly forget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This observation counsels maintaining composure during disputes so as not to lose clear thought and important points.
